Where it began

Mohammad Rizwan was born in Peshawar on 1 June 1992. He learned the game with a taped-up tennis ball before moving on to club cricket with Islamia College and the Shama Club. By 2007 he was in Peshawar's under-19 side.

His first-class career began with Peshawar in the 2008-09 season, and he hit the ground running with five fifties in his first seven innings, four of them unbeaten. That caught the eye of Basit Ali, who signed him for Sui Northern Gas Pipelines. His 224 in the 2014-15 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy final helped them win it.

The player

His Test debut came against New Zealand in November 2016, and it did not start well: he was out first ball. A regular place took a while to come, and the 2020 tour of England was the turning point. He made 161 runs in the series, kept wicket very well and was named Pakistan's player of the series, settling the gloves on him for years to come.

In February 2021 he made his first Test hundred, 115 not out against South Africa, and was again player of the series. In August 2024 he made 171 not out and 51 against Bangladesh at Rawalpindi, top-scoring in both innings. He also led Pakistan in two Tests. By November 2026 he had played 47 Tests, scoring 2,682 runs at 37.77 with three hundreds and 14 fifties, and claimed 126 catches and 10 stumpings behind the stumps.

What made him special

Rizwan was as useful with the bat as with the gloves. He became only the second wicketkeeper, after Brendon McCullum, to make hundreds in Tests, one-day internationals and T20 internationals. He set the record for T20 international runs in a calendar year, and in December 2021 he became the first batter to make 2,000 runs in all T20 cricket in a single year.

Test hundreds came along at a gentler pace than his white-ball runs. Fourteen fifties against three hundreds is a ratio his teammates might tease him about, though his 171 not out at Rawalpindi showed what could happen once he got going.

Away from the middle

2021 was his year. The ICC chose him as its T20I cricketer of the year, Wisden named him among its Cricketers of the Year, and he captained Multan Sultans to their first Pakistan Super League title. He later led Pakistan's one-day and T20 sides, signed for Sussex, and was in demand with teams in Bangladesh, the Caribbean and Australia.

And finally

Golden duck in his first Test innings; Wisden Cricketer of the Year five years later. There can be few better arguments for patience. In a one-day international against Australia in 2024 he held six catches, equalling the world record, which suggests the gloves were well worth the wait too.
